title: Estate Attorney Guide to Probate Documents (September 2026)
summary: A September 2026 guide to probate documents for estate attorneys, from opening filings and Letters Testamentary to creditor notices and tax forms.
body_markdown:
Probate is a court-supervised proceeding. From the opening petition through the final distribution order, each stage has a defined document set. This guide covers key topics that are relevant for estate attorneys, including: what documents typically open a probate estate, how Letters Testamentary and Letters of Administration work, inventory and appraisal requirements, creditor notice obligations, tax matters, and more.


**Key Takeaways**


- Three documents open many matters: the certified death certificate, the original will, and the petition for probate.
- In many states, the estate inventory is due within four months of Letters being issued.
- Both written notice to known creditors and newspaper publication are required in many states.
- Distributing assets before the creditor claim window closes can leave the personal representative personally liable for payable claims.
- Elayne organizes client intake, estate records, and asset search across 100+ financial sources.


## What Probate Documents Are and Why They Matter


[Probate is a court-supervised proceeding](https://www.elayne.com/resources/what-is-probate-court) that validates a will, appoints a personal representative, and authorizes the distribution of a decedent's estate to rightful heirs and beneficiaries. Every stage runs on paperwork. From the opening petition to the final accounting, the court requires specific documents, filed in the right form, at the right time, with the right supporting evidence.


{{blog-cta-attorneys}}


## Documents Needed to Open a Probate Estate


Three documents often anchor probate's opening:[the certified death certificate](https://www.usa.gov/death-certificate) , the original will, and the petition for probate.


In general, the certified death certificate is required by institutions the personal representative works with. Many matters need multiple certified copies since financial institutions, title companies, and government agencies often retain the copy submitted to them.


The original will must be filed with the court; a photocopy is generally insufficient. If the original cannot be located, the attorney faces a separate evidentiary proceeding to prove its contents before the matter can proceed. When there is no will, the proceeding moves to administration under intestate succession statutes.


## The Petition for Probate and Supporting Forms


The petition for probate is the foundational filing that opens a matter before the court. It identifies the decedent, the proposed personal representative, and the estimated value of the estate, along with a statement of whether the estate qualifies for simplified procedures or requires full administration.


In California and other states, the petition must be accompanied by the Notice of Petition to Administer Estate, which is served on heirs and beneficiaries and published in a newspaper of general circulation once a week for two successive weeks. Publication triggers the creditor claim window and gives interested parties an opportunity to object before the court schedules a hearing.


The Duties and Liabilities of Personal Representative form must be executed and filed by the proposed personal representative before Letters are issued, confirming the fiduciary's understanding of their obligations, including the duty of loyalty, the prohibition on self-dealing, and personal liability for breach.


## Letters Testamentary and Letters of Administration


Court-issued Letters Testamentary or Letters of Administration grant the personal representative legal authority to act on behalf of the estate. Without them, financial institutions, title companies, and government agencies have no obligation to recognize that authority.


[Letters Testamentary](https://www.elayne.com/resources/what-are-letters-testamentary) go to the named[executor](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/information-for-executors) once the will is admitted to probate. Letters of Administration are issued when there is no will and the court appoints an administrator under intestate succession statutes. A third variant, Letters of Administration with Will Annexed, applies when the named executor is unable or unwilling to serve.


## The Estate Inventory and Appraisal


The[probate estate inventory](https://www.elayne.com/resources/how-to-list-assets-and-debts-for-the-court-during-probate) documents every asset subject to the court's jurisdiction and assigns a date-of-death value to each one. It covers real property, financial accounts, physical personal property, business interests, and any asset held in the decedent's name alone or subject to probate administration.


In California, a court-appointed probate referee assigns values to most non-cash assets. The personal representative files the Inventory and Appraisal form with the referee's valuations attached. Cash equivalents are valued by the personal representative directly.


Filing deadlines vary by state but are typically within four months of Letters being issued.


## Creditor Claims and the Notice to Creditors


The[Notice to Creditors requirements](https://www.elayne.com/resources/notice-to-creditors-requirements) are a statutory mandate in every state's probate code. The notice can be direct contact with a known creditor or a public notice published in a local newspaper by the executor.


Most states require both: written notice to known creditors and publication in a newspaper of general circulation. Publication often runs three to four consecutive weeks, with the creditor claim window running concurrently for three to four months from publication.


Creditors who miss the statutory deadline may lose the right to collect, though the consequence varies by state. Some states bar the claim outright; others allow late claims against undistributed assets only.


Distributing estate assets before the creditor window closes, or failing to publish notice at all, can leave the personal representative personally liable for payable claims.

## Tax Documents


Three federal tax filings commonly intersect with a probate matter, each with a different purpose and threshold.


Form Purpose Who Files 2026 Threshold


Form 1040 Decedent's final personal return Personal representative or surviving spouse All decedents with filing income


Form 1041 Estate income tax return Personal representative Estate income above $600


Form 706 Federal estate tax return Personal representative Gross estate above $15 million


The final Form 1040 covers income earned through the date of death; the personal representative signs as fiduciary. When a refund is due and there is no surviving spouse, Form 1310 is required to claim it.


Form 1041 is required when estate income exceeds $600 during administration and continues annually until the estate closes.


Form 706 applies when the gross estate exceeds $15 million. The nine-month filing deadline is statutory; a six-month extension is available but does not extend the time to pay. Attorneys routinely condition final distribution on receiving an IRS closing letter.

## FAQ


### Can an executor be held personally liable for distributing estate assets too early?


Yes. Distributing estate assets before the creditor claim window closes, or failing to publish the Notice to Creditors at all, can leave the personal representative personally liable for payable claims. Courts treat premature distribution as a breach of fiduciary duty, and an asset that surfaces after distribution may expose the executor to claims from creditors or beneficiaries.


### What is the difference between Letters Testamentary and Letters of Administration?


Both are court-issued documents that authorize a personal representative to act on behalf of the estate. Letters Testamentary go to the named executor after the will is admitted to probate. Letters of Administration are issued when there is no will and the court appoints an administrator under intestate succession statutes. A third variant, Letters of Administration with Will Annexed, applies when the named executor cannot or will not serve.


### Does every estate need to go through probate?


No. Assets with a named beneficiary (such as life insurance or retirement accounts), assets held in joint tenancy, and assets held in a trust generally pass outside probate. Assets titled in the decedent's name alone and lacking a transfer mechanism are subject to the probate court's jurisdiction. Many estates include a mix of probate and non-probate assets.


### How long does the creditor claim window typically stay open?


The creditor claim window varies by state but commonly runs three to four months from the date the Notice to Creditors is published. Creditors who miss the statutory deadline may lose the right to collect, though the consequence depends on state law: some states bar late claims outright, while others allow them only against undistributed assets.


### What triggers Form 706 federal estate tax filing?


Form 706 is required when the gross estate exceeds the federal filing threshold, which is $15 million per individual in 2026. The filing deadline is nine months from the date of death, with a six-month extension available. The extension does not extend the time to pay any tax owed. Attorneys typically condition final distribution on receiving an IRS closing letter confirming the estate's tax obligations are resolved.


### What is a Supplement to Clear Probate Notes?


A Supplement to Clear Probate Notes is a filing the attorney submits to respond to deficiencies identified by the court examiner. Before scheduling a hearing, the examiner reviews the petition and flags anything missing, incorrect, or legally insufficient. The supplement addresses each flagged item by number. In Los Angeles County, probate notes are posted online through the court's case access portal before the scheduled hearing date.
